method:
The estimate is built from three bottom-up components, then checked against analyst reports. No main vendor files segment revenue (ION, SSI, Cultura/Constellation, Ever.Ag, Bushel and Quoreka are private or do not break the segment out), so the vendor-sum leg uses headcount-based and third-party revenue estimates instead of filings.

(A) Agricultural CTRM. ComTech Advisory is the one analyst that states its method. It sizes the market bottom-up from vendor revenue, using vendor data, published financials, headcount and announced deals, with a strict CTRM scope that excludes ERP modules, logistics-only tools and treasury (Issuu preview of the 2024 report, opened). Its 2026 report gives about $2.14B for the global CTRM market. I saw that figure only in search snippets of the CTRM Center and PRWeb releases, because the CTRM Center pages returned 403 and the release I opened had no figures. The agricultural and softs share is about 15% in ComTech's agri report snippet and about 24% in a secondary aggregator snippet. That gives roughly $320-510M. Cognitive Market Research's $475M for 2025 (page opened) falls inside this range, but its regional split (49% APAC, 11.6% US) looks unreliable.

(B) Grain, elevator and ag-retail accounting ERPs, which ComTech's scope excludes. Vendor estimates: SSI/Agvance about $25-35M (about 155 staff), Cultura (AGRIS, AgVision and others) about $30-50M (140-250 staff, $37M third-party estimate), Ever.Ag crops/grain share $30-50M of about $105M, Bushel about $39M (third-party estimate), iRely ag share $15-30M, and the long tail (AgTrax, Vertical, AgriChain, AgriDigital, EU Agrarhandel and negoce ERPs, Brazil's TOTVS and Senior agro modules) $100-250M. Total $260-500M. Intel Market Research puts grain accounting software at $770M for 2024 (page opened, no stated method), which I treat as inflated.

(C) Commodity-job share of global merchants' ERP estates (SAP Commodity Management and ECC maintenance, hosting and vendor services at ADM, Cargill, Bunge, LDC, COFCO, Viterra, Wilmar, Olam and similar), plus post-trade platforms such as Covantis: about $100-280M, a judgement call.

A+B+C comes to about $0.7-1.3B. Adding the two analyst figures ($475M + $770M = $1.25B) lands at the top of that range, consistent with analysts inflating.

Legacy share: I define legacy as in the earlier research, meaning pre-2005 client-server grain and ag-retail cores (AGRIS, the Windows Agvance core, AgTrax, Merchant Ag, AgVision), 1990s CTRMs (ION TriplePoint, Openlink Endur, Allegro) and SAP ECC estates. Estimates by tier: about 50-70% of agri CTRM spend goes to ION's legacy products (ION says 300+ agri organisations use them), with the rest at cloud-era Quoreka/Eka, Agiboo and AgriChain. About 65-85% of grain ERP spend is legacy. Hosting does not count as replacement: Agvance's subscription tier wraps hosting around the Windows core, and SSI reported in 2021 that over 60% of users were on it. Bushel is an overlay, not a replacement. About 50-80% of merchant ERP spend is still on ECC-era estates, given ADM's unfinished worldwide ERP rollout. The weighted result is 55-75%.

method:
I built the range three ways. The vendor-revenue sum is the main one. The other two are a per-passenger cross-check and analyst reports, which I used only as a ceiling. FX assumptions: EUR/USD about 1.13 and USD/CNY about 7.2 (2025 averages, my assumption).

(1) Vendor-revenue sum for FY2025 filings:
- Amadeus Air IT Solutions: EUR 2,345.9m, about $2.65bn (FY2025 management review, opened). This segment also includes Airport IT, Airline Professional Services and upsell modules (revenue management, digital commerce, NDC). I count $1.9-2.4bn as PSS-core spend.
- Sabre IT Solutions: $554.0m (Q4 2025 8-K, opened). The segment is now airline-only after the Hospitality sale in Q3 2025, but it also covers commercial/operations and agency products. I count $0.40-0.55bn.
- TravelSky aviation information platform services: RMB 4,616m, about $0.64bn (from a search snippet; the results PDF returned 403). This mixes airline-hosted PSS (ICS), CRS distribution and airport DCS. I count 40-70%, so $0.26-0.45bn.
- Hitit: about $42m. Derived from its 2025 release: EBITDA $17.9m at a 43% margin, and R&D $20.6m at 49% of revenue.
- IBS iFly Res: $0.03-0.07bn. This is my estimate, since IBS's total revenue is only about $190m in third-party data.
- Long tail: $0.3-0.6bn. This covers SITA Horizon/Gabriel, DXC SHARES (United), Unisys, Sirena-Travel, KIU, Videcom, InteliSys, Nira, ISA and FLYR. These are not disclosed, so the figure is my estimate. SITA's total revenue of $1.71bn is mostly airports and network, not PSS.
- In-house z/TPF licences, maintenance and hosting at remaining self-hosted carriers: $0.05-0.15bn (estimate).
- Sum: about $3.0bn to $4.3bn.

(2) Per-passenger cross-check. T2RL tracks 1,138 active airlines boarding about 4.99bn passengers in 2025. Implied vendor yields are about EUR 1.04 (about $1.18) per passenger boarded for Amadeus, including airport and upsell revenue. For Sabre it is about $0.80, if its 695m passengers-boarded metric is the IT Solutions count; the filing does not label it. Blended $0.6-0.9 per passenger across 4.99bn passengers gives $3.0-4.5bn.

(3) Analyst reports, used as a ceiling only:
- Verified Market Reports: $6.5bn (2025). It is internally inconsistent, because its regional rows sum to about $13.8bn.
- Search-snippet figures: $7.5bn (2025) and $7.54bn (2022).
- Market.us: $10.84bn (2024). Its scope includes services such as check-in, baggage and kiosks, and it reports a 56.7% on-premise share.
- None of these states a bottom-up method tied to vendor revenue, so I treat them as inflated by scope.

Final range: $3.0-4.5bn.

Legacy share. The earlier research names these as legacy: Altea, Navitaire New Skies/Open Skies, Sabre host/SabreSonic, Radixx, SITA Gabriel/Horizon, Videcom, Travelport/in-house z/TPF. Together they carry almost all of Amadeus's passenger-boarded revenue (PB is defined as passengers on Altea Res+Inv or New Skies). They also carry most of Sabre IT Solutions, SITA and the long tail. What I treat as non-legacy:
- Amadeus Nevio, Navitaire Stratos and SabreMosaic. These are early-stage and small, mentioned only as an incremental driver.
- FLYR, IBS iFly Res and Hitit Crane.
- TravelSky, which is not named in the research. The low bound treats it as non-legacy, along with upsell modules sold on top of legacy hosts.

That gives a legacy share of 75-90%.

method:
The range is external vendor spend on sell-side trading, OMS/EMS, clearing and post-trade, broker back-office and exchange/CCP technology. It excludes market data, internal staff, buy-side asset-management software and clearing services such as Apex or Pershing. I triangulated it three ways.

(1) Sum of vendor revenues from filings. Broadridge GTO, FY Jun-2026 10-K: Capital Markets $1,184.2M plus Wealth & Investment Mgmt $731.8M, $1.92B in total. GTO houses the BPS back office and the post-trade and Itiviti trading lines. FIS Capital Market Solutions, 2025 10-K: $3,196M. That segment also covers buy-side, treasury and lending, so I counted only 30-45%, about $1.0-1.4B. Nasdaq Capital Markets Technology, 2025 10-K: $1,091M (market tech for 135+ marketplaces, Calypso, trade management services). NRI Securities, FY Mar-2025: JPY 145.7B, about $0.95B (the THE STAR shared broker back office plus securities SI). Iress Global Trading & Market Data: A$124.8M in H1 2025, about $0.16B a year. Hundsun: CNY 5.78B in 2025, of which I counted 40-55% as brokerage cores, about $0.3-0.45B. Murex: EUR 791M (Wikipedia, year not stated) against EUR 454M (Craft), so $0.5-0.9B. ION Markets/Fidessa: private, estimated at $0.8-1.2B with no filing. The named list sums to about $6.7-8.1B. Adding a long tail of $2-4B gives $9-12B. The tail covers Bloomberg sell-side, LSEG post-trade and exchange tech, TCS BaNCS, Finastra, SS&C sell-side, Trading Technologies, FlexTrade, Koscom, Kingdom, Daiwa IR, Hitachi/NTT Data broker systems, 63 moons (about $28M), MPC, FSS and others.

(2) Top-down from Opimas, the only analyst source with a stated scope (six capital-markets areas, top-40 vendors ranked by known and estimated revenue). Total capital-markets tech spend was $163B in 2023, $48B of it external software. The buy side is about two-thirds of the total. Sell side plus execution venues therefore gets about $16B of external software. Taking 55-75% of that for trading/clearing/back office gives $9-12B in 2023, or about $10.5-14B in 2025 at Opimas's ~8% growth. As a cross-check, Opimas puts sell-side OMS alone (internal plus external) at about $6B in 2025.

(3) Commodity analyst reports, which have weak methodology and likely run high: securities trading software $7.1B (Dataintelo 2025) and post-trade processing $6.1B (TBRC 2025). They overlap, and their simple sum is about $13B, so I used them only as a ceiling check.

Result: $10-14B for 2025.

Legacy share uses the research's S1 definition: pre-cloud cores dating from before 2005. The named systems on their own come to about 8-12% of spend. That covers Broadridge BPS (mainframe, run by Kyndryl to 2031; I estimate it at 50-60% of GTO, about $1.0-1.15B), 63 moons ODIN/DOME (about $0.03B), MPC S21 and FSS FLEX (each under $0.05B). ASX CHESS is in-house, so little of it shows up as vendor spend. Other pre-2005 lineage cores raise the share to roughly 25-35%. Those are NRI THE STAR, FIS legacy securities processing, Fidessa (1981 lineage), Hundsun's older broker cores, and Nasdaq/MillenniumIT legacy exchange stacks. Hence 0.15-0.35. The low end leans on the named systems and the high end on the broader pre-2005 definition. These splits are my own estimates; no filing breaks them out.

Scope: money banks, credit unions, fintech issuers and acquiring banks pay outside vendors for card management, authorization, switching and issuer or wholesale-acquirer processing. That covers licences, maintenance, outsourced or hosted processing, SaaS and vendor services. It leaves out scheme or network fees, merchant-facing acquiring revenue and the issuer's own staff.

(A) Analyst sizes:
- Growth Market Reports puts issuer processing at $17.6B in 2024 (software, hardware and services; multi-phase primary and secondary method; 7.2% CAGR, so about $18.9B in 2025).
- MarketIntelo puts the card issuing platform market at $14.2B in 2025. Its splits look unreliable (for example 70% cloud).
- A search snippet for MAK Data Insights gives card issuance systems at $18.7B in 2025. I did not open it.
- I set aside "payment processing solutions" reports ($56-141B for 2025). They include merchant acquiring and are far outside this job.
- The analyst band is roughly $14-19B.

(B) Bottom-up from 2025 filings, with my own allocation of the card-software share in brackets:
- TSYS / FIS Total Issuing: $2.16B adjusted net revenue in FY2025. Under FIS it booked $666M GAAP in Q2 2026, about $2.6B annualized.
- Fiserv Issuing segment: $3.284B. It includes card production, print, prepaid, government and student-loan processing, so I counted about $1.8-2.5B as card processing.
- Fiserv debit processing inside Digital Payments ($3.945B in total): about $1.0-1.5B, my estimate.
- Fiserv Merchant 'Processing' (wholesale back-end processing for acquirers, $1.089B): about $0.5-1.0B.
- FIS card and debit processing before the TSYS deal: about $1.0-1.5B. Not broken out; my estimate.
- Nexi Issuing Solutions: €851.6M for 9M25, about €1.14B FY, roughly $1.1-1.3B.
- Worldline Financial Services: €792M, of which issuing and acquiring processing is about $0.45-0.6B.
- ACI Payment Software (BASE24 and related): $942M, about $0.7-0.9B relevant.
- Jack Henry card processing (inside a $873M Payments segment): about $0.3-0.5B. Part of it is resold from a third-party processor, so it overlaps.
- Marqeta: $0.62B.
- SoFi Technology Platform / Galileo: about $0.44B (search snippet, 9M = $327.8M).
- Visa and Mastercard issuer-processing services (Visa DPS and similar): about $0.5-1.5B.
- Long tail: Asia (NTT Data, FSS, UnionPay-linked, Chinese vendors), HPS, OpenWay, Network International, Thredd, i2c, Zeta, M2P, CoreCard and others, plus IBM mainframe and hosting costs at in-house TS2 and VisionPLUS licensees: about $3-6B.
- The bottom-up totals about $13.5-21B. Both methods overlap at roughly $14-22B.

Legacy share: Most incumbent revenue runs on the named legacy systems: TS2 (TSYS), Optis, FirstVision and VisionPLUS (Fiserv), BASE24 (ACI), BASE2000 (FIS), PowerCARD (HPS) and Way4 (OpenWay). The same goes for incumbent debit and EFT platforms, Nexi's and Worldline's platforms still in migration (Worldline says 55% of volume is on its target platform) and in-house mainframe licensees. Incumbents together are about $10-14B of the total. I then subtracted three things:
- cloud-native challengers (Marqeta, Galileo, Thredd, Pismo, Zeta, i2c, M2P, Highnote), about $1.5-2.5B;
- the incumbents' own modernized products (VisionNext, ACI Connetic, Worldline's target platform);
- non-legacy long-tail vendors.
That leaves roughly 60-80% on legacy.

Main uncertainties:
- the card share of Fiserv's segments and of FIS's pre-TSYS business, which I allocated myself;
- Asia and in-house mainframe spend, which no filing covers;
- whether wholesale acquirer processing belongs in scope. It adds about $0.5-1B.

method: Triangulated two ways for 2025. (1) Analyst market sizes. Three reports were opened, and their 2025 figures were USD 1.72B (The Business Research Company, base year 2025, CAGR model), USD 2.00B (Future Market Insights, 61.3% solutions and 38.7% services, 58.7% cloud and 41.3% on-prem) and USD 2.64B (Precedence Research, 72.4% cloud, North America 42.4% = USD 1.12B). Search snippets gave other 2025 figures of USD 2.12B to 2.66B (Market Research Future, Verified, WiseGuy), but those pages were not opened. None of them publishes a bottom-up method. Their vendor lists also include Intuit/QuickBooks, Xero, Procore and Deltek, which makes the scope generous. (2) A bottom-up sum of vendor revenue, mostly estimates because the core vendors do not report segment figures. Trimble Viewpoint (Vista, Spectrum, Jobpac): Trimble guided about USD 200M non-GAAP revenue for 2019 in its 2018 8-K. It no longer breaks Viewpoint out. AECO segment revenue was USD 1,498.6M in 2025 and growth there is about 10%/yr, which compounds to roughly USD 300-400M. Sage construction (Sage 300 CRE, Sage 100 Contractor, Sage Intacct Construction) is not disclosed and is estimated at USD 200-350M from 15k+ claimed CRE customers and maintenance pricing. Foundation is about USD 65M (ZoomInfo estimate) and could be up to about USD 150M. CMiC is about USD 75.5M (GetLatka estimate). COINS/Access is about USD 75M (Crunchbase-type estimate seen in a search snippet). CGC eCMS is about USD 20-30M and Jonas construction brands about USD 100-200M, both my estimates. Construction-vertical modules on Acumatica, NetSuite, Deltek ComputerEase, Premier, Adaptive, Eque2, RedSky and Causeway add about USD 150-250M. These named construction-accounting vendors sum to roughly USD 1.1-1.5B in licence, subscription and maintenance revenue. Adding VAR and implementation services (FMI puts services at about 39% of the market) brings it to roughly USD 1.4-2.0B. Contractors' share of QuickBooks and Xero, the construction-firm share of SAP/Oracle ERP, and non-US local vendors (RIB, Nevaris, Asian packages) add more. Procore (USD 1,323M 2025 revenue) is excluded: it integrates with the accounting system rather than replacing it, and including it would double-count. The final range is USD 1.6B to 2.6B. The low end is the bottom-up sum plus services. The high end is the top analyst figure (Precedence). Legacy share: the legacy systems named in the earlier research are Sage 300 CRE, Vista, Spectrum, Jobpac, Foundation, CMiC, eCMS, Jonas, COINS, Oracle EBS/SAP at contractors, Eque2, RedSky and Causeway. Together they account for roughly USD 0.85-1.0B of vendor revenue (about USD 0.9B on midpoint estimates), plus most of the VAR and services spend around them. Non-legacy spend comes from Sage Intacct Construction, Acumatica and NetSuite construction, QuickBooks and Xero used by small contractors, and new entrants (Adaptive, Archdesk, Briq). That gives legacy about 50-70% of spend. Analyst on-premise shares (27.6% Precedence, 41.3% FMI) are a floor, not the answer. Most Vista and Spectrum customers now run in Trimble-hosted single tenancy (Trimble Construction One), which analysts count as cloud even though the product is the legacy client-server codebase. Biggest uncertainties: no vendor discloses construction-accounting revenue directly. The Viewpoint and Sage figures are extrapolations, and CMiC, Foundation and COINS figures are third-party estimates.

Scope: core banking and ERP for credit unions, US community banks, cooperative and rural banks, and MFIs or SACCOs. Includes licences, subscriptions, maintenance, and hosted or outsourced core processing. Digital banking, card and payments processing are excluded where a vendor reports them separately. Internal IT staff are excluded. Captive cooperative IT companies (Atruvia, Allitude and others) are counted as vendors because they are separate entities that bill the member banks. The French and Dutch cooperative mega-groups, Brazil's Sicoob and Sicredi in-house IT, and Rabobank and OP in-house IT are excluded.

(A) Vendor and utility revenue sum, in USD:
- US, $2.6-3.7bn. Jack Henry Core segment was $739M in FY2025 (to 30 Jun 2025). It serves about 715 Symitar credit unions plus 520 SilverLake, 260 CIF 20/20 and 170+ Core Director banks, about $440k per core client. Fiserv does not split out core revenue (Financial Solutions totalled $9.66bn in 2025). Fiserv holds about 42% of banks (KC Fed, 2022) and 1,254 of 4,631 credit unions (Dec 2024). Scaled on Jack Henry's per-client revenue, that is an estimated $1.2-1.8bn. FIS community-bank cores are estimated at $0.2-0.4bn. Others (CSI, COCC, Corelation, FedComp, Finastra, CU*Answers, Sharetec, plus Symitar CUSOs) are estimated at $0.5-0.8bn. Cross-check: about 250M accounts at $10-20 each gives $2.5-5bn.
- Europe cooperative IT utilities, $1.1-2.0bn. Revenues sum to about EUR 2.4bn: Atruvia AG EUR 1.7bn (2024), BCC Sistemi Informatici EUR 330M, Allitude EUR 275M and RSI EUR 117M. I assume 40-70% of that is core or ERP rather than workplace IT, payments and back office.
- Japan and Korea, $0.6-1.2bn. Shinkin SSC had JPY 22.2bn revenue (FY to Mar 2025) and Nochu Information Systems (JA Bank, JASTEM) JPY 32bn. Add direct NTT Data spend, shinkumi, and Korean MG, Shinhyup and Nonghyup locals.
- Canada and Australia mutuals, $0.2-0.4bn.
- India, $0.15-0.3bn. The PACS ERP is Rs 2,516 cr over 5 years. Add UCB, DCCB and StCB core banking.
- Indonesia BPR, Philippine rural banks, Vietnamese People's Credit Funds and Malaysian and Thai co-ops, $0.1-0.25bn. Roughly 1,500 BPR and 370 rural banks at $20-60k each.
- MFIs, SACCOs and LatAm co-ops, $0.2-0.5bn. Mambu's total 2024 revenue was $129M, of which only part falls in this segment.
- Total: about $5.0-8.4bn.

(B) Analyst cross-check. Global core banking software was $16.7bn (SNS, 2025) to $19.3bn (Fortune, 2025), and large banks hold about 38% (SNS). Taking 25-35% for credit unions, community, cooperative and rural banks gives $4.5-6.5bn. Add microfinance software at $1.2bn (2024; it overlaps) for an analyst-implied $5-8bn. Fortune puts US core banking at $5.3bn (2024), and about half of that to community banks and credit unions (about $2.7bn) matches the US vendor sum. The analyst reports give little methodology and project 12-16% CAGRs, so I weight the vendor sum more.

Legacy share: nearly all spend runs on the systems named in the category research or their equivalents. These are Fiserv and Jack Henry cores (US incumbents take about 85-90% of US spend), agree21, the other European utilities' cores, JASTEM and the SSC mainframes, USSI and ARB+, OMNIEnterprise, and local PowerBuilder and client-server cores. Cloud-native challenger spend is roughly $0.4-1.0bn: Mambu, Nymbus, Oradian, Temenos SaaS for MFIs, M2P, BSP-funded SaaS cores in the Philippines, and Corelation counted generously. That gives 80-92% legacy. One caveat: the NABARD PACS ERP is named in the earlier research but is a new 2023+ build. If it is excluded from legacy the share moves by under 1 point.

I built the range three ways.

(1) Analyst market sizes. The six 2025 figures I found run from $10.9B to $20.1B: Proficient $10.86B, Market Research Intellect $11.88B, Precedence $13.79B, SNS $16.73B, Custom Market Insights $17.94B, Fortune Business Insights $19.30B and Straits $20.12B. None of the pages I opened states a usable methodology. Precedence splits its figure about 65% solutions and 35% services, and both it and Fortune say on-premise is the largest deployment. I treat these numbers as inflated toward the high end.

(2) Vendor filings, core-attributable revenue for FY2025:
- FIS Banking Solutions: $7,285M (10-K). It covers core, digital and payments. Assuming 30-40% is core gives $2.2-2.9B.
- Fiserv Banking business line: $2,435M (10-K disaggregation table). It covers account processing, digital banking, risk and check processing. Assuming 55-75% is core gives $1.3-1.8B.
- Jack Henry Core segment: $739M (FY to June 2025).
- Temenos: total revenue $1,071M. Product revenue is $943M (subscription and SaaS $452.5M plus maintenance $490.3M), and core banking is about 81% of it. With a share of services, that is about $0.85B.
- Oracle Financial Services Software: revenue Rs 7,672 crore (about $0.88B) for FY to March 2026. Assuming 50-65% is FLEXCUBE and banking gives $0.45-0.6B.
- Silverlake Axis: RM783.5M (about $0.17B), FY2024.
- Finastra Universal Banking, Infosys Finacle and TCS BaNCS do not disclose revenue. I estimate them at $0.4-0.6B, $0.3-0.4B and $0.3-0.5B.
- Challengers: Mambu about $129M (2024, third-party estimate) and Thought Machine £47.6M (2024).

The named vendors sum to about $6.7-8.6B. Adding a long tail (Japanese and Chinese bank IT vendors, Avaloq, CSI, DXC Hogan, Sopra and others, about $2-4B) gives $9-12.5B of packaged-vendor spend. Third-party implementation and SI services plus hosting and mainframe run costs for core estates add about $3-7B. The total is about $12-19B.

(3) Ceiling check. Temenos's 2025 annual report sizes all third-party banking software product spend (subscription, SaaS, term licence and maintenance, not only core) at about $23B for FY24 and $25B for FY25. That puts core product spend at roughly half to two-thirds of it, consistent with the range above.

Legacy share. The earlier research names essentially every incumbent core as legacy: FIS Systematics/IBS, Fiserv Premier/DNA/Signature, the Jack Henry cores, Temenos Transact/T24, Finastra Equation/Midas, Silverlake SIBS, FLEXCUBE, Finacle, BaNCS and SAP. Non-legacy is cloud-native cores: Thought Machine, Mambu, 10x, Pismo, Finxact, Zeta, FIS MBP and the like, plus the implementation services spent migrating to them. Challenger licence and SaaS revenue is about $0.5-1.0B, and the migration services attached to them are about $1-2B. Out of $12-19B, that leaves about 80-92% of spend on legacy systems.

Caveats:
- The core share of FIS and Fiserv revenue is my assumption, not disclosed.
- The Finastra, Finacle, BaNCS and long-tail figures are unverified estimates.
- Bank in-house staff costs are excluded per scope.
- The FY periods differ slightly between vendors (June 2025, December 2025, March 2026).

I built the range two ways.

(A) Analyst market sizes for court case management software. The credible cluster runs from about $1.0B to $2.0B:
- Business Research Insights: about $0.96B for 2026 (search snippet only).
- QYResearch/Valuates: $1.08B for 2024 (search snippet only; the page fetch failed).
- Verified Market Research, "court management software": $1.20B for 2025 (search snippet only).
- Mordor Intelligence: $1.96B for 2025. I opened this page. It covers software platforms, not implementation services, puts North America at 39.7% and says cloud is 64.7%.

(2) Vendor revenue. Few vendors disclose this segment. Deloitte holds at least $5B in eligibility contracts across 25 states. Spread over multi-year terms (Tennessee $823M, Pennsylvania $541M, Georgia $528M), that is about $0.7-1B a year. (3) Bottom-up agency external IT spend for 2025.

- China Golden Tax IV: RMB 5.7B build cost, excluding operations.

Dataintelo's "tax administration software" figure ($8.3B in 2024) mixes government and enterprise buyers. Neither report discloses a usable methodology, so both are low-weight.

Business Research Insights and Verified Market Reports put the market at $2.86B for 2025 or 2026, which is below IBM's Transaction Processing line alone. Their methodology statements are boilerplate. LEGACY SHARE: this category is itself the legacy stack: z/OS, CICS, IMS, Db2 for z/OS and VSAM, ClearPath, Fujitsu, and CA and BMC mainframe tooling. Almost all of the spend therefore keeps those systems running. The parts that are not legacy are small:
- modernization and migration tooling such as watsonx Code Assistant for Z, AWS Transform and the Rocket and Micro Focus rehost products
- Linux on Z workloads
- cloud rehosting

At roughly 35-45% retail, that is about $5-6B for retail POS software. Retail-only POS software reports give $14.7B (Virtue) and $16.3-16.6B (Market Research Intellect). Neither states a methodology, so I treat them as inflated ceilings. Merchandising, category, planning and inventory software adds roughly $2-5B: Spherical Insights puts category management at $2.0B (about 40% of it merchandising), and TechSci puts retail inventory software at $1.7B. Top-down total: about $8-12B, with an outer ceiling near $20B if you take the retail-POS reports as given.

(2) Gartner cross-check. Gartner's 1Q25 forecast gives $205B of enterprise IT spending in retail for 2025. This figure comes from the search snippet of the Gartner document page, which returned 403 when opened. An unverified secondary snippet says about 28% of retail IT spend goes to software, which gives about $57B. If POS plus merchandising is 15-25% of that, the result is about $9-14B.

(3) Bottom-up from vendor filings. Revenue figures are from filings and results. The splits that strip out hardware are my estimates.
- NCR Voyix Retail segment: $1.842B in FY2025, with software ARR of $783M company-wide. Excluding hardware, about $1.2-1.4B.
- Toshiba TEC Retail Solutions: JPY 333.6B (about $2.2B) for the year to March 2025, holding about 2.82M installed POS units. Software and maintenance at 35-45% gives about $0.8-1.0B.
- Diebold Nixdorf Retail: $1.008B in 2025. Software and services at about 45% gives about $0.45B.
- Oracle Retail, including Xstore and RMS: not disclosed. Estimated at $0.8-1.2B.
- SAP retail (IS-Retail/S/4 Retail): not disclosed. Estimated at $0.4-0.8B.
- Blue Yonder: $1.42B in total, of which about 15-25% is merchandising and planning, so about $0.2-0.35B.
- GK Software: EUR 194M (about $0.21B).
- Aptos including LS Retail: estimated at $0.2-0.35B.
- Lightspeed: subscription revenue $371M, with retail at about half, so about $0.15-0.2B.
- Shopify: offline revenue $748M, which is mostly payments and hardware. POS subscriptions estimated at about $0.1-0.2B.
- Long tail: Flooid, Enactor, Jumpmind, Retail Pro, Epicor Eagle, Microsoft D365 Commerce, RELEX/o9 merchandising, Square retail, and Chinese, Japanese and Indian local vendors. Estimated at $2-4B.
The named vendors come to about $4.7-6.4B. Adding the long tail gives about $7-10B, and vendor and partner implementation services add about $2-4B. Bottom-up total: about $9-14B.

The three methods overlap at about $9-14B. I widened the top to $16B to allow for under-counted Asian SMB POS and SI services. Final range: $9-16B for 2025.

Legacy share. "Legacy" means the systems in the earlier research: 4690/SurePOS ACE, JDA MMS on IBM i, on-prem Oracle RMS and Xstore, the NCR legacy portfolio, the Aptos/Epicor heritage suites, Microsoft Dynamics RMS, LS Nav, SAP IS-Retail on ECC, and homegrown IBM i systems. The evidence:
- A 2026 Aptos/Coresight survey of 150 global retail executives found 22% on hybrid or fully on-prem POS, and another 36% on cloud-hosted systems without cloud-native capability. That makes 58% not fully modernised. 30% run systems at least five years old.
- NCR Voyix's FY2025 10-K still reports revenue from its legacy retail portfolio and says contracts can hinder sunsetting it.
- Datos Insights counts about 440k new POS installs in the year to June 2025 and forecasts 2.3M over five years. That is slow turnover against Toshiba's roughly 2.8M installed units alone.

Spend runs heavier on the legacy side than counts of retailers suggest. Tier-1 grocery and mass retailers concentrate maintenance spend on legacy cores, while SMB spend skews cloud. I therefore put legacy at 35-55% of spend: below the survey's 58% not-modernised figure, because some cloud-hosted Xstore and RMS deployments are not legacy by the earlier definition, and above the 22% that are strictly on-prem.

Caveats:
- No analyst report with a stated methodology isolates retail POS plus merchandising.
- Oracle, SAP and Aptos revenue for this segment are estimates.
- The software and services share of hardware vendors' segments is estimated.
- Payments revenue (Shopify, Lightspeed, NCR) is excluded.

method:
I used three methods.

(1) Analyst market sizes for 2025, low to high: Grand View $3.4B (search snippet; the page returned 403), Fortune $3.88B, Mordor $4.04B, MarketsandMarkets $4.57B (top-down plus bottom-up triangulation), Persistence $4.7B and Straits $4.85B. Gartner states its methodology and is the most conservative. It says WMS software 'exceeded $3B in 2024' (Gartner 2025 MQ via Made4net) and in 2022 forecast 'over $4B by 2026' at a 13%+ five-year CAGR (Gartner 2022 MQ reprint). That puts 2021 at about $2.2B and 2025 at about $3.4–3.6B. I read Gartner's figure as software (licence, subscription, maintenance) only, without vendor professional services, so vendor services would add to it. Mordor's '80% services' split looks unreliable and I did not use it.

(2) Bottom-up sum of WMS revenue for the main vendors, around 2025, including the vendors' own services:
- Manhattan: about 50% of $1,081M = ~$540M (FY25 8-K; WMS share from a Tech Fund interview note)
- Blue Yonder: ~$300–350M. Gartner gave WMS software of $160M for 2021 (reprint) and $223M for 2023 (snippet only), plus services, out of $1.42B total FY25 revenue.
- Oracle: ~$300–350M. Gartner gave $280M WMS software for 2023 (snippet only).
- SAP EWM plus LE-WM: ~$400–600M, my estimate. SAP does not disclose it. Gartner counts about 7,000 WMS customers, of which 2,250+ are EWM.
- Infios/Körber: ~$300–350M of its $500M+ total, which includes MercuryGate TMS
- Infor: ~$150M. Gartner put Infor's SCE at $189M in 2021.
- Tecsys: ~US$127M (C$176.5M, FY25)
- EPG: ~$100M (WMS $84M in 2021)
- Generix: ~$60M (53% of $83.5M in 2021)
- Reply, Mecalux, Made4net, Mantis, Softeon and other Magic Quadrant vendors: ~$150–250M

That comes to about $2.6–2.9B. A long tail adds $0.6–1.2B: Chinese and Japanese vendors, Hardis Reflex, PSI, ERP-embedded WMS and SMB SaaS such as Deposco, Logiwa, Extensiv and Unicommerce. Total: about $3.3–3.9B.

(3) Cross-check: Manhattan's ~$540M WMS revenue at a ~20% market share implies about $2.7B.

Range chosen: $3.3B (vendor-sum floor) to $4.6B (Gartner software plus vendor services, close to the MarketsandMarkets figure). Third-party systems-integrator fees are excluded.

Legacy share: weighted by vendor, using the systems named in the earlier research.
- Manhattan: maintenance $130M plus licence $15M is 13% of total revenue. Applied to its WMS revenue (WMi, WMOS, SCALE), legacy is about 30%. 98% of its RPO is cloud.
- Blue Yonder: only ~70 of 973 WMS customers were on SaaS in 2021, so legacy is about 60% of its WMS revenue.
- SAP: LE-WM still makes up a large part of the ~7,000 customer base, so about 45%.
- Infor: 60% of WMS customers were on legacy Infor WMS (Gartner 2022), so about 60%.
- Körber/HighJump: cloud adoption was 5–79% depending on product, so about 55%.
- Oracle: EBS WMS against WMS Cloud, about 35%.
- Long tail: about 20%.

That gives about 34%. Mordor puts on-premises at 44.8% of 2025 revenue (cloud 55.2%), which is an upper bound because it also counts on-prem EWM and other non-legacy products. Range: 30–45%.
